candidate_relations.reason: The patient had no urticaria, asthma, angioedema, or pruritus and normal peripheral eosinophils, while inflammation was localized to breast lobules and ducts.
Biopsy explicitly found no granulomata and instead showed eosinophil-rich perilobular and periductal chronic inflammation.
No diabetes is reported and the specimen lacks the dense keloidal fibrosis and lymphocytic lobulitis typical of diabetic mastopathy.
The developing asymmetry was composed of marked eosinophil-rich inflammation rather than cysts, apocrine change, or stromal fibrosis of fibrocystic change.
No malignancy was found, so this is a benign breast condition, but the phrase omits the defining eosinophilic mastitis histology.
Although lymphocytes were present, the infiltrate was enriched in eosinophils and no dense stromal sclerosis was described.
The biopsy supports a benign lesion, but only the perilobular and periductal eosinophil-rich infiltrate identifies eosinophilic mastitis.
The pathology report specifically states that granulomata were absent, which conflicts with idiopathic granulomatous mastitis.
Inflammation was perilobular and periductal but contained no granulomas, excluding idiopathic granulomatous lobular mastitis.
No storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, or IgG4-positive plasma-cell assessment is reported in the eosinophil-rich biopsy.
The mixed infiltrate is chronic mastitis, but the generic term loses the diagnostically dominant eosinophils and idiopathic localized presentation.
The biopsy had no granulomata and there are no pulmonary, nodal, or systemic findings of sarcoidosis.
Peripheral eosinophil levels were normal and hypereosinophilic syndrome was excluded, so idiopathic eosinophilia is not the localized breast diagnosis.
The absence of atypia makes the process benign, but this label does not communicate the eosinophil-predominant mastitis responsible for the mammographic asymmetry.
Twelve vacuum-assisted cores showed chronic inflammatory cells without malignant epithelium or another cancerous population.
Idiopathic eosinophilic infiltration of the breast describes the same localized eosinophil-rich perilobular and periductal mastitis after systemic allergic and hypereosinophilic causes were excluded.
Seasonal allergic rhinitis is the only atopic history, but the patient lacked active allergic symptoms and it does not itself constitute the breast inflammation.
The lesion is confined to breast lobular and ductal tissue, with no painful limb induration, eosinophilia, or fascial pathology.
Chronic inflammatory breast disease covers the tissue response but omits the eosinophilic predominance that distinguishes this asymptomatic mammographic lesion.
Normal peripheral eosinophils and absence of asthma, vasculitis, neuropathy, or systemic organ disease argue against Churg-Strauss syndrome.
